title: Why do senior developers avoid scattering null checks?
shortTitle: Why do senior developers avoid scattering null checks?
keyPoints: Scattered null checks clutter code and hide business logic
Use Optional as a return type to force callers to handle absence
Use Objects.requireNonNull() at API boundaries to fail fast with a clear message
Prefer empty collections (List.of()) over null to represent 'no data'
Null Object pattern: return a no-op implementation instead of null

s1_definition.oneliner: Senior developers prevent nulls at the boundary instead of checking them everywhere. Use Optional for return types, requireNonNull for parameters, and empty collections instead of null.
s1_definition.profdef:
Strategies to minimize null checks:

- **Optional return types:** Force the caller to handle absence.
- **requireNonNull at boundaries:** Fail fast at entry points.
- **Empty collections:** `List.of()` instead of returning null.
- **@NonNull annotations:** Static analysis catches nulls at compile time.
- **Null Object pattern:** Return a no-op object instead of null.
s1_definition.analogy: Instead of checking every desk in the bank for missing forms (null checks everywhere), the mailroom rejects missing forms at the front door (boundary validation) and replaces empty envelopes with blank template forms (empty collections / Null Object).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Scattered null checks:  if (x != null) { if (x.y != null) { ... } }  → cluttered

  Better patterns:
    Boundary:  Objects.requireNonNull(x, "message")  → fail fast
    Return:    Optional<Account>                      → caller handles
    Collection: List.of() instead of null             → safe to iterate
    Annotation: @NonNull → static analysis            → compile-time warning
    Null Object: return NoOpLogger instead of null    → no checks needed
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Senior developers prevent nulls at the boundary instead of checking everywhere. Use requireNonNull at API entry points, Optional for return types, empty collections instead of null returns, and @NonNull annotations for static analysis.

One sentence to remember: validate at the boundary, return Optional for absence, use empty collections not null – prevent nulls instead of checking them.
